Symptoms include fever, chills, malaise and myalgia, with rectal, low back, or peri- neal pain. There is often bacteriuria with frequent and ur- gent dysuria. The prostate is enlarged, tender, and warm.1,2 Chronic bacterial prostatitis (category II) is relatively rare, and may develop from acute bacterial prostatitis in some men. It is characterised by pelvic pain and recurrent uri- nary-tract infections. The prostate appears to be normal but in some cases is swollen or firm.1 Bacterial prostatitis should be managed with appropriate antibacterial therapy2-4 (see under Urinary-tract Infections, p.199). Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (catego- ry III), which has also been described as abacterial prosta- titis, is the most common form of prostatitis. The aetiology and pathogenesis remain unclear, and suggestions have in- cluded infection with atypical organisms that cannot be de- tected by conventional techniques, intraprostatic reflux, or immunological processes.1 Neurological5 or psychologi- cal factors1,5 may also play a role in some patients. Symp- toms of chronic pelvic pain syndrome include pelvic, peri- neal, and genital pain, lower urinary-tract symptoms, sexual dysfunction, and general symptoms such as head- ache and fatigue.1 In inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome (category IIIA), leucocytes can be found in ex- pressed prostatic secretion, in the urine after prostatic mas- sage, and in semen; no leucocytes can be detected in non- inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome (category II- IB; previously called prostatodynia).1,5 There are no universally effective treatments for chronic pelvic pain syndrome; treatment trials overall have been small and of poor quality.2,4-6 Many clinicians favour ini- tial management with antibacterials despite negative cul- tures, in order to treat occult atypical infection.2 An oral fluoroquinolone is the antibacterial of choice (or a tetracy- cline for patients allergic to fluoroquinolones). Recom- mended duration of treatment varies, but courses are gen- erally of 4 to 8 weeks, depending on response in the first few weeks.2,3,5 However, there is no strong evidence to support this practice,6 and although there are some studies to suggest that antibacterial treatment may be beneficial in inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome, there is less evidence for the non-inflammatory form.3 Other treat- ments that have been tried, with variable results, include2,4-6 the 5α-reductase inhibitor finasteride, alpha blockers such as alfuzosin, terazosin, or tamsulosin, pen
